title: The history of the immune system
tagline: From plague survivors in Athens and smallpox scabs in China to cowpox, eating cells, antibodies, and the end of smallpox and polio in India.
intro: For thousands of years people noticed that surviving some diseases protected you from them, and some cultures risked a mild dose to stay safe. Jenner turned that into the first vaccine. Then microscopes and experiments revealed the army behind it: eater cells, antibodies, T cells and B cells that learn and remember. That knowledge wiped out smallpox, drove polio out of India, and produced COVID-19 vaccines in less than a year.

eras.name: Surviving once
eras.summary: Plague survivors, and variolation in China, India, Turkey and West Africa: a risky mild dose to prevent a deadly one.

eras.name: The first vaccines
eras.summary: Jenner’s cowpox, Pasteur’s weakened germs, Metchnikoff’s eating cells, antitoxins, and Haffkine’s vaccines in India.

eras.name: Finding the army
eras.summary: Allergy, antibiotics, clonal selection, T cells, dendritic cells and monoclonal antibodies.

eras.name: Wiping diseases out
eras.summary: Smallpox eradicated, HIV found, India’s Universal Immunisation Programme and the long fight against polio.

eras.name: Vaccines at speed
eras.summary: mRNA vaccines, and COVID-19 vaccines including India’s Covaxin, made in under a year.

events.title: Survivors don’t catch it twice
events.text: During a terrible plague in Athens, the historian Thucydides noticed that people who recovered could nurse the sick safely, because the disease never attacked the same person twice, at least not fatally.
events.why: It is one of the oldest written notes of immunity: surviving a disease can protect you from it.

events.date: 16th century (the earliest reliable accounts; some claim older)
events.title: Blowing smallpox scabs up the nose
events.text: Chinese doctors ground up dried scabs from mild smallpox cases and blew the powder into a healthy child’s nose. The child usually got a mild illness and was then protected. Historians date reliable accounts to the 1500s; claims of a much older practice are uncertain.
events.why: Deliberately giving a mild dose of a disease, called variolation, was the first attempt to train the immune system.

events.title: Variolation reaches Europe and America
events.who: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu; Onesimus and Cotton Mather
events.text: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had seen variolation in Constantinople and had her daughter inoculated in London in 1721. In Boston the same year, an enslaved West African man, Onesimus, told Cotton Mather how it was done in his homeland, and inoculation was tried during an epidemic.
events.why: Knowledge from Turkey and West Africa brought the idea to Europe and America.

events.date: described 1767; how old the practice was is disputed
events.title: Tika: variolation in Bengal
events.who: Inoculators described by J. Z. Holwell
events.text: A British doctor, John Zephaniah Holwell, described travelling inoculators in Bengal who scratched smallpox matter into the skin and then cared for the patient. Some writers claimed the practice was ancient, but no old Sanskrit text describing it has been found, so its age is uncertain.
events.why: It shows variolation was spread across Asia before vaccines existed.

events.title: Cowpox protects against smallpox
events.text: Jenner scratched material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid’s hand into the arm of eight-year-old James Phipps. Weeks later he exposed the boy to smallpox, and Phipps did not fall ill. Cowpox is Latin vacca, cow, which gave us the word vaccine.
events.why: It was the first vaccine: a mild, related germ that trained the body to resist a deadly one.

events.title: India’s first vaccination
events.text: Smallpox vaccine lymph reached India in May 1802, carried along a chain of vaccinated people. A three-year-old girl in Bombay, Anna Dusthall, became the first person in India to be vaccinated, on 14 June 1802.
events.why: Vaccination arrived in India just six years after Jenner’s experiment.

events.title: Cells that eat invaders
events.text: Watching see-through starfish larvae under a microscope, Metchnikoff pushed rose thorns into them. The next morning, moving cells had crowded around the thorns. He named such cells phagocytes, “eating cells”, and argued they defend the body.
events.why: It was the discovery of innate immunity: neutrophils and macrophages at work, like the splinter in chapter 2.

events.title: Weakened germs make vaccines
events.text: Pasteur found that old, weakened chicken cholera germs protected hens (1879). He made an anthrax vaccine for sheep (1881), and on 6 July 1885 his team gave a rabies vaccine to nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog. He survived.
events.why: Pasteur showed vaccines could be made on purpose in the lab by weakening a germ.

events.title: Antitoxin: blood that fights a poison
events.who: Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō
events.text: Von Behring and the Japanese scientist Kitasato showed that the blood serum of animals that survived tetanus or diphtheria could neutralise the germ’s poison and protect other animals. Serum therapy soon saved many children with diphtheria.
events.why: It revealed antibodies in the blood, and it won the first Nobel Prize in medicine in 1901.

events.title: Cholera and plague vaccines tested in India
events.text: Haffkine tested his cholera vaccine on thousands of people in India from 1893. When plague struck Bombay in 1896, he made a plague vaccine in a makeshift lab and tried it on himself first, in January 1897. His Bombay lab later became the Haffkine Institute.
events.why: It is often called the first vaccine developed in India.

events.title: Receptors and magic bullets
events.text: Ehrlich proposed that cells carry “side chains” that grab a toxin like a lock and key, and that cells release extra copies into the blood as antitoxins. He dreamed of “magic bullets”: medicines that hit only germs. He shared the 1908 Nobel Prize with Metchnikoff.
events.why: His lock-and-key idea is how we still picture antibodies binding antigens.

events.title: Anaphylaxis: when the defence harms
events.text: Trying to protect dogs against sea-anemone poison, Richet and Portier found that a second small dose, weeks later, caused a sudden, violent reaction. They called it anaphylaxis, “against protection”.
events.why: It was the first clue that the immune system can overreact, the basis of allergy.

events.title: Penicillin, the first antibiotic
events.text: Fleming noticed that a mould growing on a dish of bacteria had killed the bacteria around it. The substance, penicillin, was turned into a medicine in the 1940s by Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and colleagues. Fleming warned that misuse could make bacteria resistant.
events.why: Antibiotics help the immune system against bacteria, but not against viruses.

events.title: BCG vaccinations begin in India
events.text: A BCG vaccine laboratory was set up at the King Institute in Guindy, and vaccination against tuberculosis began in August 1948. BCG, a weakened cousin of the TB germ, is still given to Indian babies at birth.
events.why: It began one of the world’s largest vaccination efforts.

events.title: The polio vaccine works
events.who: Jonas Salk and a trial of about 1.8 million children
events.text: A huge field trial showed that Jonas Salk’s killed-virus polio vaccine was safe and effective. Albert Sabin’s weakened, oral vaccine followed, and oral drops later became the main tool of India’s Pulse Polio campaign.
events.why: Polio, which paralysed hundreds of thousands of children a year, could now be stopped.

events.title: Clonal selection: the right cell multiplies
events.text: Burnet proposed that each lymphocyte carries a receptor of one shape. When a germ fits it, that one cell is selected and multiplies into a clone of identical cells, some of which remember the germ. Experiments soon proved him right.
events.why: It explains how the immune system learns and remembers, the heart of chapters 3 and 4.

events.title: What the thymus is for
events.text: Doctors had long thought the thymus was useless. Miller removed it from newborn mice and found they could not reject skin grafts or fight infections well. The thymus, he showed, makes the lymphocytes later called T cells.
events.why: It found where T cells are trained.

events.title: The scouts are found
events.text: Looking at mouse spleens under the microscope, Steinman spotted cells with long branching arms and named them dendritic cells. He showed they are the scouts that wake up T cells. He won the 2011 Nobel Prize, awarded days after his death.
events.why: It explained how the adaptive immune system is switched on.

events.title: Monoclonal antibodies
events.text: Köhler and Milstein fused an antibody-making B cell with a cancer cell that never stops dividing. The hybrid made endless copies of one single antibody. They chose not to patent it, so labs everywhere could use it.
events.why: Monoclonal antibodies are now used in pregnancy tests, COVID tests and many cancer and arthritis medicines.

events.title: India’s last smallpox case
events.who: India’s National Smallpox Eradication Programme with WHO
events.text: After a massive search-and-contain campaign, with health workers visiting every village to find cases and vaccinate everyone around them, India recorded its last case of smallpox in 1975. India was declared smallpox-free in 1977.
events.why: India, once home to most of the world’s smallpox cases, had beaten the disease.

events.title: Smallpox is wiped out
events.text: After the last natural case, in Somalia in 1977, the World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated. A disease that killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone was gone.
events.why: It is still the only human disease ever eradicated, proof that vaccines plus herd immunity work.

events.title: The virus behind AIDS is found
events.text: Barré-Sinoussi and Montagnier found a new virus in a lymph node from a patient. It was later named HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus. It infects helper T cells. They shared the 2008 Nobel Prize.
events.why: Knowing the cause led to blood tests and, later, medicines that control HIV.

events.title: The Universal Immunisation Programme
events.text: India expanded its 1978 Expanded Programme on Immunization into the Universal Immunisation Programme, covering six diseases at first. Today it offers free vaccines against 12 diseases to about 2.67 crore newborns and 2.9 crore pregnant women each year.
events.why: It is one of the largest public health programmes in the world.

events.title: India’s first HIV cases are found
events.who: Suniti Solomon and her student Sellappan Nirmala
events.text: Dr Suniti Solomon and her student tested blood samples in Madras and found India’s first confirmed HIV infections. Solomon went on to set up care and counselling for people with HIV and fought the stigma around it.
events.why: It started India’s response to HIV, which now includes free treatment for everyone who needs it.

events.title: Pulse Polio: two drops for every child
events.who: Government of India, WHO, UNICEF, Rotary and millions of volunteers
events.text: India held its first national polio immunisation day, giving oral polio drops to every child under five on the same day, at booths, bus stands, railway stations and homes. The drives were repeated for years.
events.why: Reaching every child at once cut off the virus’s chances to spread: herd immunity in action.

events.title: A trick that makes mRNA vaccines possible
events.text: Karikó and Weissman found that swapping one building block of mRNA kept it from setting off alarm bells in the immune system. Their work, long ignored, made mRNA vaccines practical. They won the 2023 Nobel Prize.
events.why: It let scientists design a new vaccine in days once a virus’s genes were known.

events.title: India’s last case of wild polio
events.text: A young girl in Howrah district, West Bengal, was paralysed by wild poliovirus. She was India’s last case. As recently as 2009, India had 741 cases, the most in the world.
events.why: Many experts had thought India would be the hardest place on Earth to beat polio.

events.title: India is certified polio-free
events.text: After three years with no wild polio cases, the WHO certified the South-East Asia Region, including India, polio-free. Children in India still get polio vaccine, because the virus survives in a few other countries.
events.why: It showed that high vaccine coverage can wipe a disease out even in a huge, crowded country.

events.title: The first COVID-19 vaccines
events.text: Less than a year after the new coronavirus was identified, 90-year-old Margaret Keenan became the first person to receive an approved COVID-19 vaccine outside a trial. Vaccines made in several ways followed within weeks.
events.why: It was the fastest vaccine development in history, built on decades of earlier work.

events.title: Covaxin, India’s own COVID-19 vaccine
events.who: Bharat Biotech with ICMR and the National Institute of Virology
events.text: On 3 January 2021 India’s drug regulator approved Covaxin, a killed-virus vaccine made in India, and Covishield, made by the Serum Institute of India, for emergency use. India’s vaccination drive began on 16 January 2021 and gave more than two billion doses.
events.why: India made and gave vaccines on a scale few countries could match.

people.name: Edward Jenner
people.note: Made the first vaccine, from cowpox.

people.name: Louis Pasteur
people.note: Weakened germs on purpose to make vaccines against anthrax and rabies.

people.name: Élie Metchnikoff
people.note: Discovered phagocytes, the cells that eat invaders.

people.name: Kitasato Shibasaburō
people.note: Co-discovered antitoxin with von Behring and grew the tetanus germ in pure culture.

people.name: Waldemar Haffkine
people.note: Made cholera and plague vaccines in India and tested them on himself first.

people.name: Frank Macfarlane Burnet
people.note: Explained how the immune system learns with clonal selection.

people.name: Suniti Solomon
people.note: Found India’s first HIV cases and built care for people living with HIV.

people.name: Katalin Karikó
people.note: With Drew Weissman, made mRNA vaccines possible.

series.title: Wild polio cases in India each year
series.caption: Confirmed wild poliovirus cases (National Polio Surveillance Project, via GPEI, CDC and Indian J Community Med). Cases rose and fell in outbreaks until coverage got high enough, then dropped to zero.

facts: The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow, because the first vaccine used cowpox.
Your marrow makes about 100 billion new neutrophils every day, and most live for only about a day.
Smallpox is the only human disease ever eradicated. Polio is close: wild polio now survives in only two countries.
Measles is so contagious that about 19 in every 20 people must be immune to stop it spreading.
Köhler and Milstein chose not to patent monoclonal antibodies, which now earn billions as medicines.
